Sunday, 18th October, at the trattoria "Da Graziella". At the table: Graziella, Pietro, Signor Franco, Matei and Giulia. Giulia puts a little parcel next to Matei's plate.
So, Giulia… it seems to me you have something to say.
A present? But it isn't my birthday… A bib? "Little restorer"? I think it's one of Pietro's jokes.
It wasn't me! I think it was Grandma!
It wasn't me. But I think I know who it was.
Matei, it's not a joke. In May there'll be three of us.
Three? You mean… you're pregnant? I can't believe it! Since when have you known?
For a week. I'm sorry you were the last to know, but I wanted to tell you in a special way.
The last? So Graziella already knew? And Pietro?
I only knew about the cradle! I think Grandma found out from Grandma Assunta, at the wedding.
In my opinion it's the best news anyone has heard in this trattoria in fifty years.
But… what about Syracuse? And the Caravaggio?
I think the Caravaggio has already waited four hundred years. It can wait a little longer.
I agree. And now, everyone to the table: in my opinion, someone who's expecting a baby has to eat for two!
"mi sembra che" = it seems to me that
"saremo in tre" = there'll be three of us
Double BB and "ya" run together: AB-bya, AB-bya-no. Stress on the first syllable.
GL + I = a soft "ly": ba-va-LYEE-no, as in "figlio".
A mio parere è un capolavoro.
Mi sembra che tu sia stanca.
"Secondo me" is followed by the INDICATIVE (Secondo me è vero), but "credo che" by the SUBJUNCTIVE (Credo che sia vero). Don't mix them: NOT "Secondo me sia vero".
When the subject is the same, use "di + infinitive": "Credo di sapere" (I think I know), NOT "Credo che io sappia".
2. The congiuntivo passato: how to form it
It's formed like the passato prossimo, but the auxiliary (avere / essere) is in the present subjunctive. Verbs with ESSERE make the participle agree:
In the singular all three persons are identical. That's why the pronoun is often added: "Credo che tu abbia ragione."
Present subjunctive = the action happens NOW or in the future. Past subjunctive = the action happened BEFORE:
Credo che Giulia sia stata stanca ieri.
In English you say "I think it was". In Italian: "credo che SIA STATO", NOT "credo che è stato" (a very common mistake, even among Italians in fast speech — but in the exam it counts!).
As with the present subjunctive (chapter 26), emotions, wishes and doubts require the subjunctive — and the past one if the event has already happened:
I'm sorry you were the last to know.
I doubt Bellini understood straight away.
It's strange that nobody said anything.

That Sunday afternoon Matei and Giulia made more phone calls than in the whole year. The first was to Sibiu. Doina answered on the second ring, heard the news and said nothing for a whole minute. Matei thought the line had gone dead. Then he heard his mother crying and, in the background, his father asking: "What's happened? Who's died?"

"Nobody's died, Ion!" Doina shouted. "Quite the opposite!" Five minutes later Ion was already in the cellar looking for the bottle of pălincă he kept "for a really special occasion". It was three in the afternoon. Ilinca, who was on duty at the hospital, sent a message of just one word, in capital letters: "MĂTUȘĂ!!!", that is, aunt. A minute later she sent another: "And I'm going to be the godmother. That's not a question."

The second call was to Naples. Rosaria screamed so loudly that Matei had to hold the phone away from his ear. Then she passed the phone to Grandma Assunta. "I knew it," the old lady said calmly. "I've known since the wedding. A Neapolitan bride who doesn't drink even one glass of wine at her own wedding? I thought straight away there was a cradle on the way. But I didn't tell anyone."

"Grandma," said Giulia, "I think you told Graziella at least." Silence. "Well," Assunta admitted, "Graziella, yes. But Graziella isn't 'anyone'. Graziella is family." Giulia laughed. It seems to me, she thought, that in this story nobody has ever been able to keep a secret, except Totò.

The hardest problem, though, was another one: Bellini. On Monday morning Giulia arrived at the workshop half an hour early, made coffee for the professor, tidied the brushes and rehearsed her speech ten times in her head. Matei wanted to come with her, but Giulia said no. "I think I have to do this alone. It was my decision."

Bellini came in at nine on the dot, saw the coffee already made and stopped. "Esposito," he said suspiciously. "Coffee made, brushes tidied. I have the impression you have some bad news for me." "It's not bad, Professor," said Giulia. "But it is news. In May I'm going to have a baby. So I can't go to Syracuse in February."

The professor said nothing. He sat down at his desk and drank his coffee slowly, all of it, to the last drop. Giulia waited, standing, her heart pounding. She thought Bellini was angry. She thought he would give the Caravaggio to someone else. She thought she had lost his trust.

Then Bellini opened a drawer and took out an old black-and-white photograph. A man with a moustache was holding a small child in his arms in front of an enormous painting. "My grandfather Ernesto," he said. "And the child is me, in 1966. My grandfather took me to work when my mother was ill. According to him, that's where I learned not to touch anything."

He put the photograph on the table in front of Giulia. "Esposito, I think you've made the right decision. And I also think the Caravaggio has waited four hundred years without complaining. It can wait seven more months." He picked up the phone. "Hello? Syracuse? Bellini here. We're postponing the restoration to September. No, it's not a question of money. It's a question of cradles."

When he hung up, Giulia had tears in her eyes. "Thank you, Professor. I don't know what to say." "Then don't say anything," he replied. "But I'm warning you: I think this child will become a restorer. With two parents like you, poor thing, it has no choice at all." And for the first time in three years, Giulia saw Bellini laugh.

That evening Matei came home with a little parcel. Inside was a tiny new brush with a light wooden handle. "For the little restorer," he said. "That way, when it grows up, it'll have its own. But I think I'll have to teach it Ernesto's rule: 'Look. And don't touch anything.'" Giulia put the brush next to Ernesto's old one, on the shelf above the bed. They were almost the same. One was fifty years old. The other hadn't been born yet. Matei turned off the light and, for the first time in weeks, they fell asleep straight away, all three of them.
